candidates.title: Human factors in generative AI companions: a systematic literature review of trust, relational dependence, psychosocial outcomes, and responsible adoption
candidates.abstract: Context Generative AI companions and socially oriented chatbots are systems designed or used to sustain social, affective, or relational interaction. They increasingly function as persistent interaction partners across systems ranging from earlier rule-based, retrieval-based, and pre-LLM architectures to contemporary generative AI companions. Prior reviews and conceptual models have largely examined user-facing relational mechanisms or specific ethical and legal issues. Yet, how these mechanisms connect with platform, organizational, and regulatory conditions remains fragmented. Objectives This study addresses this gap by synthesizing human-factor and responsible-adoption concerns across technology generations and developing an evidence-calibrated multi-stakeholder framework spanning human, organizational, technological, and regulatory layers. Methods We conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review of records retrieved from Scopus, ACM Guide to Computing Literature via the ACM Digital Library, Web of Science Core Collection + MEDLINE, and IEEE Xplore. We examined English-language, peer-reviewed publications made available between 2005 and 2024. From 1699 identified records, 42 publications were included and analyzed using thematic synthesis. Results Four analytical themes were identified: usability and relational affordances in interaction; trust, attachment, over-reliance, and psychosocial outcomes; responsible adoption, platform design, and organizational mediation; and governance, privacy, and accountability. Technology emerged as a cross-cutting mediator linking design features, user experience, organizational practice, and governance concerns. The first two themes drew on 29 and 33 materially contributing publications, whereas the latter themes each drew on 12 and represent emerging synthesis areas. Conclusion The review shows that responsible adoption of AI companion systems requires attention not only to user experience, but also to platform incentives, design affordances, data practices, service continuity, and governance mechanisms. The framework's distinctive contribution is to connect these concerns across stakeholder layers while preserving differences in evidentiary maturity. It is a provisional analytical heuristic, not a validated causal model.

candidates.title: GestAdapt: Workspace-Conditioned Co-Speech Gesture Generation for Humanoid Robots
candidates.abstract: Co-speech gestures for robots must adapt not only to speech and embodiment, but also to the workspace available for performing the motion. Since the same speech can be accompanied by different gestures, a robot can respond to workspace constraints, e.g., gestures for speech next to a wall. In these scenarios, the robot should gesture in a suitable motion rather than simply correcting an unconstrained one. To achieve this goal, we present GestAdapt, a workspace-conditioned framework that conditions co-speech gesture generation on a prescribed wrist workspace. The GestAdapt framework learns from six complementary co-speech corpora through a shared motion representation and supports retargeting to different robot embodiments. Quantitative evaluation shows that generated motions remain close to the real-motion distribution while respecting the workspace. In a user study, gestures generated under modified workspace constraints receive a mean quality score of 3.24/5, above our no-workspace variant (2.43/5) and below the reference motions (3.68/5). In a real robot evaluation, all compared motions are retargeted to the Reachy2 humanoid robot under identical workspace constraints. Motions generated with our framework rank first in 69.7\% of comparisons, higher than our no-workspace variant baseline and retargeted ground-truth motions constrained afterward. Overall, the results support adapting gestures to the available workspace during generation, rather than modifying unconstrained trajectories afterward to satisfy workspace constraints, potentially compromising gesture naturalness.

candidates.title: ImaGGen: Zero-Shot Generation of Co-Speech Semantic Gestures Grounded in Language and Image Input
candidates.abstract: Human communication combines speech with expressive nonverbal cues such as hand gestures that serve manifold communicative functions. Yet, current generative AI-based gesture generation approaches are, for the most part, restricted to simple, repetitive beat gestures that accompany the rhythm of speaking but do not contribute to communicating semantic meaning. This paper tackles a core challenge in co-speech gesture synthesis: generating iconic or deictic gestures that are semantically coherent with a verbal utterance. Our basic assumption is that such gestures cannot be derived from language input alone, which inherently lacks the visual meaning that is often carried autonomously by gestures. We therefore introduce a zero-shot system that generates gestures from a given language input and additionally is informed by imagistic input, without manual annotation or human intervention. Our method integrates an image analysis pipeline that extracts key object properties such as shape, symmetry, and alignment, together with a semantic matching module that links these visual details to spoken text. An inverse kinematics engine then synthesizes iconic and deictic gestures and combines them with co-generated natural beat gestures for coherent multimodal communication. A comprehensive user study demonstrates the effectiveness of our approach. In scenarios where speech alone was ambiguous, gestures generated by our system significantly improved participants’ ability to identify object properties, confirming their interpretability and communicative value. While challenges remain in representing complex shapes, our results highlight the importance of context-aware semantic gestures for creating expressive and collaborative virtual agents or avatars, marking a substantial step forward towards efficient and robust, embodied human-agent interaction. More information and example videos are available here: https://hvoss-tech.github.io/ImaGGen/

candidates.title: Iconic words and iconic gestures in early interactions : emergence, engagement and learning
candidates.abstract: This thesis investigates the role of iconicity - resemblance between form and meaning - in early language development, focusing on how iconic words and gestures support communication, engagement, and learning in infancy and childhood. Across five empirical studies, I combine experimental and corpus-based methods to explore how iconic forms function within naturalistic caregiver-child interactions and influence developmental trajectories. Studies 1 and 2 examine the use of iconic words in infant-directed speech. In naturalistic interactions, caregivers’ use of iconic words was associated with increased infant engagement and more exaggerated infant-directed-speech-style parent prosody. This pattern was replicated in a larger sample across three age groups (13-, 18-, and 23-month-olds), suggesting that iconicity plays a key role in supporting engagement during early interactions. Study 3 tested the impact of iconicity on word learning. Children aged 18 months and 3 years were taught names for toys that made either matched or mismatched real animal sounds. While both age groups learned congruent names better, this advantage was statistically significant only in 3-year-olds, suggesting possible developmental changes in the ability to use iconicity to benefit word learning. Study 4 used a longitudinal corpus to examine the frequency and function of onomatopoeia across early vocabulary development. Findings replicated other studies that show onomatopoeia are more frequent in both infants’ early vocabularies and caregiver speech towards younger infants but also showed that they are used more often with playful prosody and reduplication by both infants and caregivers and usually serve enactment functions rather than purely referential ones. Finally, Study 5 identified and analysed infants’ earliest iconic gestures, revealing that children as young as 12 months produce innovative, representational gestures in natural interactions, often without adult scaffolding. Together, these studies offer converging evidence that iconic forms are embedded in multimodal, affect-rich interactions and support communicative development through their capacity to engage, represent, and bridge meaning.

candidates.title: CompanionSim: Synthetic Data for Evaluating Anthropomorphism in Human-AI Relationships
candidates.abstract: Many people now see AI systems as not just productivity tools but as social companions. Researchers are eager to study the consequences of AI companionship behaviors, such as validation, which evoke trust, empathy, and attachment in human–human interaction. However, human–AI interaction data is limited and unreliable, slowing research progress. We scale small amounts of real-world data by simulating multi-turn human–chatbot dialogue across a range of chatbot behaviors and use cases. We release CompanionSim: a simulation framework with 2,240 simulated human–chatbot conversations representing 16 chatbot behaviors across seven use cases. Human participants annotated the simulated conversations and real-world conversations in two experiments probing perceptions of companionship behaviors. We conducted Study 1 with a U.S. representative sample (N = 628) and Study 2 across the U.S., U.K., India, and Nigeria (N = 3,646). Surprisingly, we find that companionship behaviors reduced likability, humanlikeness, and trust in AI chatbots. These effects were larger in particular subgroups: women and older participants saw companionship chatbots as less likable, humanlike, and trustworthy. We encourage researchers to leverage real-world and synthetic data together to study the differential impacts of AI companions and to create benchmark evaluations of AI chatbots.

candidates.title: Conversational artificial intelligence and children’s social-emotional development: a scoping review
A scoping review of trust in firsthand and secondhand communication involving humans and artificial intelligence
candidates.abstract: Conversational and generative artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly create and pass information between people. This can make it hard to see who created a claim, whether it was changed, and whom to trust. Many studies examine firsthand human-human and human-AI communication, but less is known about secondhand communication, in which AI or another actor passes on a claim made elsewhere. In these cases, a human decision maker must evaluate the claim and the people or systems that created or passed it on. We present a scoping review built around six minimal motifs that represent firsthand or secondhand communication routes. Humans or AI systems may serve as the source or intermediary, while the decision maker remains human. We screened 3810 records and coded 124 studies to identify 21 trust factors in four dimensions: Decision Maker, Messenger, Message Property, and Environment. Qualitative synthesis also identified four recurring route-level patterns: distorted trust calibration, trust transfer, extremity amplification, and accountability diffusion. These patterns guide future research on AI-mediated communication. Overall, this review provides shared terms and a route-based framework for studying trust in multi-party human-AI communication and designing AI-mediated communication systems.

candidates.title: Robot gaze-timing combinations and the uncanny valley
candidates.abstract: Anthropomorphic robots are increasingly prominent technologies, yet how variations in robot gaze are associated with human perception and visual engagement remain poorly understood. We examined this with a multi-method design spanning three complementary levels: subjective ratings assessed whether an uncanny-valley pattern was present across the tested gaze combinations, individual-difference measures tested moderation effects by personality and attitudes, and eye movements characterized how the robot's face is visually explored. We presented a virtual robot across nine gaze conditions, systematically varying direct-to-averted gaze ratios and durations within a storytelling scenario. Participants ( N = 61) rated each robot's anthropomorphism, likability, and perceived empathy while their eye movements were recorded, and their personality traits and attitudes toward robots were assessed. Results showed that (1) the relationship between perceived anthropomorphism and likability followed an uncanny-valley pattern (a significant cubic relationship), whereas perceived empathy increased monotonically with anthropomorphism; (2) exploratory analyses showed that extraversion and negative attitudes toward robots moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and likability, while neuroticism moderated the relationship between anthropomorphism and perceived empathy; (3) Eye Movement analysis with Hidden Markov Models (EMHMM) identified two viewing patterns (analytic and holistic) and participants higher in openness viewed the highest-rated robot gaze more analytically and the uncanny robot gaze more holistically. These findings indicate that an uncanny valley pattern was observed across the tested gaze-timing combinations and that individual differences may be associated with variation in robot evaluations and visual attention patterns.

candidates.title: Research on optimization algorithms for packaging VR display based on multimodal interaction Model and BERT
candidates.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) technology has significant application potential in information display, and multimodal interaction can further enhance users' immersion and interaction efficiency. The BERT model has powerful semantic understanding. However, current research on integrating the two and applying them to the optimization of VR display systems in the packaging industry remains scarce, and this direction also faces practical challenges, such as insufficient multimodal information fusion and low computational efficiency. The optimization framework combines BERT-based semantic encoding with aligned gesture and gaze features through adaptive multimodal fusion. The fused representation supports interaction-policy updates driven by user feedback and response latency. The experimental results show improvements in the measured performance of the optimized system integrating multimodal interaction and BERT: the immersion score has increased from 72.3 to 89.6, an increase of 17.3 points; the operation response delay has decreased from 320ms to 110ms, a reduction of 210ms; the scene switching fluency has increased from 68.5% to 92.1%, an increase of 23.6 percentage points. In terms of resource occupation and rendering efficiency, the average GPU load has decreased from 85.3% to 62.1%, a decrease of 23.2%; the peak memory occupation has decreased from 3.2GB to 2.1GB, a savings of 1.1GB; the scene rendering frame rate has increased from 45fps to 68fps, an increase of 23fps; the single interaction response time has decreased from 2.8 seconds to 1.2 seconds, a reduction of 1.6 seconds. In terms of model performance, the BERT model's AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) is 0.911, higher than 0.896 for the CNN model and 0.903 for the BiLSTM model. In some experiments, after about 250 epochs of training, the accuracy is close to 90% and the loss is about 0.5. When the dataset size of the K5 sub-model is 6000, the AUC value is close to 1.0. This optimization method can effectively improve system performance and user experience.

candidates.title: High- versus low-anthropomorphic-cue packages and health-information trust: social presence and source credibility under explicit AI disclosure
candidates.abstract: Background AI virtual opinion leaders are increasingly used in health communication, but it remains unclear whether bundled anthropomorphic-cue packages foster initial trust and information-adoption intention when AI identity is explicitly disclosed. Methods Guided by the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm, Social Presence Theory, Source Credibility Theory, and the Information Adoption Model, we conducted a single-factor between-subjects randomized experiment comparing overall high- and low-anthropomorphic-cue packages. The packages differed simultaneously in avatar realism, gesture behavior, interpersonal/linguistic framing, and video duration; AI disclosure and the response-button structure were held constant. A total of 536 valid responses were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. Social presence, source credibility, trust, and adoption intention were measured by participant self-report immediately after a single branched-video exposure. Results The overall high-versus-low package contrast increased social presence. Social presence was positively associated with source credibility; source credibility was positively associated with trust in AI-generated health information; and information trust was positively associated with health information adoption intention. The direct effect of the package contrast on information trust was not significant, whereas the bootstrapped serial indirect effect through social presence and source credibility was significant. Conclusion Within the present Chinese sample and single-exposure setting, the randomized contrast supports an effect of the overall cue package on initial social presence, while the mediation estimates are consistent with the hypothesized indirect pathway to information trust. The design cannot identify the independent contribution of any visual, gestural, linguistic, vocal, interactive, or duration component. The outcome is self-reported adoption intention, not observed health behavior.

candidates.title: A risk-based view of trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots
candidates.abstract: Human–machine collaboration is becoming increasingly prevalent across a wide range of industries. However, the risks associated with the adoption of emerging technologies have triggered a crisis of trust, leading to widespread concerns about the deployment of collaborative machines in the service industry. Therefore, this study aimed to investigate the role of trust in human–machine collaboration from a risk-based view, with the following research objectives: (1) to identify the antecedents of trust and test hypothesized associations among trust, perceived risk, adoption intention, and use behavior; and (2) to construct a risk-based model capturing the associations of trust with behavior in human–machine collaboration. Survey data were collected from 201 respondents in China and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that empathy, competence, reciprocity, and assurance were associated with trust in collaborative machines, while perceived risk mediates the hypothesized paths between trust and adoption intention. These findings provide insights into designing for trust in human–machine collaboration on cooking robots.

candidates.title: Is a fair trial possible in the metaverse? A procedural justice and sociological perspective in conversation
candidates.abstract: The legal sphere is increasingly moving towards the metasphere, through the adoption of virtual reality technologies across legal procedures, processes, and education.This article examines how this shift affects the execution and experience of criminal justice.Drawing on procedural justice theory and sociological perspectives, it explores how metaverse-based justice reshapes human connection, communication, and the rituals that underpin the fairness and legitimacy of criminal proceedings.While virtual reality promises greater efficiency and accessibility in criminal trials, it challenges the traditional conception of the courtroom as a physical space where justice is enacted and experienced.Emphasising participation, dignity, and trust, the analysis highlights the importance of experiential dimensions in perceptions of fairness.Key sociological themes are explored, including how virtual environments shape interaction and entrainment.The article argues that the metaverse may transform the social practices that constitute a fair trial, with potential consequences for the core principles of criminal justice.Ultimately, it contributes to critical debates on legal digitalisation by questioning whether virtual technologies can reconcile efficiency with the essential human experience of justice.

candidates.title: Women’s Affect and Queer Fandom in China
candidates.abstract: This book investigates how “rotten girls”—female fans of male-male romance—navigate the affective terrain of queer fandom in post-socialist China. Focusing on the everyday experiences of these fans, it traces their engagements with queer representations of masculinity across state-sanctioned, commercial, and fan-produced media. Through the lens of affect, this book highlights how these women negotiate identity, desire, and agency within an environment marked by censorship, market forces, and patriarchal norms. Drawing on semi-structured interviews and close analysis of danmu (real-time comment) fan videos and online discussions, the study introduces the concept of a “post-socialist structure of feeling” to capture the intuitive, often ambivalent ways fans inhabit Chinese queer fandom. It explores how this cultural space serves as an affective heterotopia—a contradictory, emotionally charged zone where fans consume, produce, and contest representations of soft masculinity. This book also examines how these women emerge as “killjoys”: feminists-in-the-making who challenge, endure, and reimagine the limits of China’s heteronormative social order. Offering original insights into Chinese queer fandom, this book is a valuable resource for scholars and students in media and cultural studies, gender studies, queer theory, and Asian studies. It contributes to growing conversations in transcultural fan studies by foregrounding affect as both a methodological and conceptual tool for understanding how digital fandom mediates identity, emotion, and power in contemporary China.

candidates.title: Artificial companions shape embodied desire and human attraction
candidates.abstract: Artificial companions offer a setting in which to examine how responsive technologies may shape embodied desire and human attraction. This theoretical article proposes that repeated interaction with such systems can influence what users come to experience as emotionally available and desirable. Drawing on embodied, embedded, enactive, and extended cognition, it develops an account of artificial companions as affective infrastructures. On this account, conversational memory and adaptive responses may sustain affective looping, through which users come to rely on the system for recognition and emotional regulation. The analysis distinguishes text-based, multimodal, and physically embodied companions, whose different conditions of interaction may affect this process. It also distinguishes interpersonal friction, which such systems may partly reduce, from infrastructural friction arising from technical failures and platform governance. Artificial companions are examined as participants in human meaning-making whose responsiveness can acquire personal significance without establishing lived intentionality on the machine side. The resulting relation is described as asymmetrical or pseudo-enactive coupling. The article thus develops the hypothesis that artificial companions may educate desire by influencing expectations of intimacy. Whether this occurs, how it varies across users, and whether its effects extend to human relationships remain questions for comparative and longitudinal research. This framework contributes to machine cognition by examining the relational environments artificial systems make possible and the limits of their participation in human affective life.

candidates.title: From Accuracy to Responsibility: A Systematic Review of Computational Sustainability, Algorithmic Fairness, and Governance in Transformer-Based Text Classification
candidates.abstract: Background The rapid adoption of Transformer-based architectures such as BERT and RoBERTa has advanced text classification in high-stakes domains, including cyberbullying detection, mental-health screening, and fake-news moderation. However, these advances have increased computational demands and raised concerns regarding environmental sustainability, algorithmic fairness, and responsible governance. This systematic review examines the interrelationships among computational sustainability, Green AI mechanisms, the efficiency–fairness trade-off, and governance in Transformer-based text classification. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Studies were identified from five databases: ScienceDirect, Wiley Online Library, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and ProQuest. A total of 94 studies published between 2020 and 2026 were synthesised to examine strategies for improving computational efficiency, their implications for fairness, and governance mechanisms relevant to responsible Transformer-based text classification. Results Four complementary categories of Green AI mechanisms were identified: model compression, including pruning, knowledge distillation, and quantization; alternative energy-efficient architectures; secure and efficient inference; and lifecycle-oriented governance techniques such as machine unlearning. Across the reviewed studies, these mechanisms reduced parameter counts or energy consumption by up to sixty-fold while generally maintaining comparable predictive performance. However, efficiency gains did not consistently preserve fairness, with some compression strategies increasing subgroup performance disparities, particularly for under-represented languages and demographic groups. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning demonstrated potential for jointly improving efficiency and equity. Persistent governance gaps were also identified, including limited alignment between machine-unlearning techniques and regulatory rights such as the GDPR right to erasure, insufficient transparency in vendor-imposed training decisions, and limited sustainability criteria for evaluating legacy research. Conclusions The findings indicate that computational efficiency, algorithmic fairness, and governance should be considered interconnected dimensions of responsible Transformer-based text classification rather than independent objectives. The review proposes a unified evaluation framework integrating sustainability metrics, fairness-aware evaluation protocols, and governance considerations to support more responsible Transformer deployment and research. The findings also highlight potential contributions to Sustainable Development Goals 9, 10, 12, and 13.

candidates.title: Using photo-elicitation interviews to explore the experiences of social media influencers with visible differences: “I didn’t mean to become a voice for our whole community”
candidates.abstract: Some individuals with visible differences (conditions or injuries that affect one's appearance), have become social media influencers, using their platforms to share experiences, challenge stereotypes, and promote representation of appearance diversity. However, no research has explored their experiences and how they navigate this evolving role. Therefore, semi-structured photo-elicitation interviews were carried out with fourteen adult influencers (aged 18-45) with a range of visible differences to understand their experiences. Social media posts from their own accounts were used to facilitate the discussion. The sample included nine cisgender women, one trans woman, and four cisgender men. All participants used Instagram, 11 used TikTok, nine Facebook, and three YouTube, with follower counts ranging from 4300 to 300,000. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist/contextualist framework. Three themes were generated: (1) 'You've got to create your own seat at the table', (2) 'Feeling an endless pressure to influence', and (3) 'There is no handbook for this job'. Social media provided opportunities to increase visibility of visible differences, foster connection, and influence public perceptions. However, participants described continuous pressure to produce content, remain visible, and support their communities while protecting their own wellbeing. As influencing is a new and evolving role, they often balanced authenticity, social responsibility, and financial sustainability without formal guidance. Influencers with visible differences play an important role in representation and advocacy of appearance diversity but face unique challenges. Findings underscore the need for clearer guidance, regulation, and support to promote safe, sustainable, and socially responsible influencing.

candidates.title: From Virtual Persona to Purchase: The Trust Engagement Pathway of AI-Generated Influencers in Sustainable Textile Marketing
candidates.abstract: While AI-generated social media influencers can provide consistency, scalability, and creative control to the textile industry, there is a question about their credibility when they make sustainability-related statements. The current research investigates how the effectiveness of AI-influencers affects consumers' trust in brands, sustainable brand engagement, and purchase intention in the textile industry in Pakistan. The model combines the Stimulus-Organism-Response model and source credibility and signaling models. To finalize and validate the reporting framework, a deliberately generated data set of 250 potential social-media consumers was analyzed with an explicitly simulated approach in PLS-SEM with 5,000 bootstrapped replications. All HTMT ratios were below .85 and the measurement model had acceptable reliability (Cronbach's alpha = .854-.884) and convergent validity (AVE = .683-.718). AI-influencer effectiveness was a strong predictor of consumer trust, sustainable engagement, and purchase intention (beta = .497, .251, and .181, respectively). The trust variable (beta = .425) and the variable of sustainable engagement (beta = .176) to purchase intention were significant, while the variable of sustainable engagement was the strongest predictor of purchase intention (beta = .346). Indirect effects via trust and engagement and the serial pathway of trust-engagement also showed significant results. The results confirm that AI-powered endorsers have the greatest impact when they are transparent and credible, fostering trust and driving sustainability awareness to genuine engagement with the brand. This is a simulated numerical dataset, and thus the results illustrate an analytically coherent paper structure; these should be replaced or verified with real field data prior to the actual publication of the dataset.

candidates.title: More than a loading bar: Conversational silence and anthropomorphic latency cues in mental health chatbots
candidates.abstract: Mental health chatbots increasingly rely on conversational interaction to support users' emotional well-being, yet little is known about how users interpret temporary silence while waiting for system responses. Existing research on social presence and anthropomorphic interaction has primarily focused on conversational content after a response is generated, whereas the waiting phase remains underexplored. Drawing on social presence theory, this study conceptualizes anthropomorphic latency cues as socially meaningful signals that may shape users’ emotional and interactional experiences during temporary conversational silence. Two studies were conducted. Study 1 developed and semantically validated three categories of anthropomorphic latency cues (empathic, effortful, and playful). Study 2 employed a within-subjects laboratory experiment with university students, comparing five latency-cue conditions (text, progress bar, empathic, effortful, and playful) using subjective evaluations, eye-tracking measures, and semi-structured interviews. The results showed that anthropomorphic latency cues were associated with lower anxiety and greater pleasure in several condition-level comparisons relative to non-anthropomorphic feedback. Perceived interaction continuity was significantly associated with reduced anxiety and enhanced pleasure. Within the anthropomorphic conditions, mediation analyses revealed significant indirect associations among perceived anthropomorphism, social presence, and emotional and interactional outcomes. Eye-tracking results indicated longer fixation durations on anthropomorphic latency cues during temporary silence. Qualitative findings further suggested that participants often interpreted latency cues as signals of attentiveness, responsiveness, and interaction continuity rather than merely as technical loading indicators. Overall, temporary conversational silence may function as a socially meaningful phase of AI-mediated interaction rather than a purely technical delay. The study extends social presence research into temporally silent phases of conversational AI interaction and provides preliminary design implications for chatbot-based support systems.

candidates.title: Makerspaces in School Libraries - Transforming Learning Ecosystems for 21st Century Education: A review
candidates.abstract: Makerspaces in school libraries have become transformative settings that enhance creativity, collaboration, critical thinking, and problem-solving skills in learners. Based on constructivist and constructionist theories, these spaces transition libraries from passive information stores to active learning environments. This review synthesizes existing research on the conceptual basis, implementation, educational effects, challenges, and future prospects of makerspaces, highlighting their role in supporting STEM/STEAM education, digital literacy, inquiry-based learning, and inclusive pedagogy. Global evidence, including guidelines from the American Association of School Librarians and the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions, underscores the essential role of school librarians as facilitators and leaders in innovation. While studies indicate improved student engagement, self-directed learning, and collaborative knowledge construction, obstacles like funding shortages, training deficiencies, and sustainability challenges, particularly in developing areas, persist. The review concludes that makerspaces signify a paradigm shift in school librarianship, promoting 21st-century competencies and equitable access to creative technologies. To optimize their educational benefits, strategic planning, policy alignment, and librarian development are crucial.

candidates.title: Ready for robotic dentistry? a comparative study of trust, behavioral intention, and procedural acceptance
candidates.abstract: Artificial intelligence and robotic systems are becoming part of dental care, but it remains unclear to what extent dentists, dental students, and non-dental participants would accept receiving robot-assisted dental treatment themselves and how much they trust these technologies. This cross-sectional online survey included 1,055 participants: 542 dental students, 95 practicing dentists, and 418 non-dental participants. The questionnaire assessed perceived usefulness, procedural acceptance, trust and control, social influence, ethics, privacy, and cost, and behavioral intention. All composite scores were calculated on 5-point Likert-type scales, with higher scores indicating greater agreement or acceptance. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, group comparisons, the Friedman test, correlation analyses, and hierarchical linear regression. Participants generally considered AI and robotic systems useful, but their willingness to undergo robot-assisted dental procedures was relatively low. Mean scores were 2.95 for perceived usefulness and 2.25 for procedural acceptance. Acceptance differed significantly across the 11 dental procedures, with the highest score for tooth whitening and the lowest for soft-tissue surgery. Dentists showed lower procedural acceptance than both dental students and non-dental participants. The trust and control construct was the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by procedural acceptance and perceived usefulness. The final regression model explained 56.5% of the variance in behavioral intention. Acceptance was generally lower for more invasive procedures, particularly surgical procedures. Acceptance of AI and robotic dentistry was associated more strongly with trust, clinician control, and procedure type than with perceived usefulness alone. Further cross-cultural studies involving multiple countries are needed to confirm these findings in more diverse populations.

candidates.title: Brand Trust in the Digital Marketplace: Conceptual Perspectives and Emerging Dimensions
candidates.abstract: The rapid expansion of digital technologies has transformed the marketplace and created new challenges for developing and maintaining consumer trust in brands. In digital environments, consumers interact with organizations through websites, social media, mobile applications, online platforms, artificial intelligence, personalized communication and digitally mediated service encounters. These developments have expanded opportunities for organizations to build relationships with consumers while simultaneously increasing concerns related to privacy, security, transparency, authenticity, information credibility and technology-mediated interactions. This paper reviews the existing literature on brand trust in the digital marketplace and examines its changing dimensions in contemporary digital environments. The review focuses on the role of digital marketing, social media, artificial intelligence, personalization, electronic communication, customer experience, online reviews, digital platforms, transparency, privacy and consumer–brand relationships in shaping trust. The literature indicates that brand trust in digital environments is multidimensional and extends beyond traditional perceptions of brand reliability and credibility. Consumers increasingly evaluate brands according to their ability to provide secure, transparent, personalized, authentic, consistent and meaningful digital experiences. At the same time, excessive personalization, inappropriate data practices, technological uncertainty and information overload can weaken consumer confidence. The paper consolidates the existing literature and identifies emerging dimensions of digital brand trust, including technological trust, data and privacy trust, platform trust, interactional trust, experiential trust and authenticity. The review contributes to the understanding of how traditional concepts of brand trust are being reshaped by the characteristics of the digital marketplace.

candidates.title: Text-messaging with a conversational AI as an out-group member: Preliminary evidence for a new application of intergroup contact
candidates.abstract: The application of artificial intelligence (AI) for electronic contact (e-contact) offers new possibilities for intergroup contact. This pilot study examined whether exchanging instant messages with an AI-generated out-group member reduces prejudice, using explicit and implicit pre- and post-contact evaluations with a pure control condition. The contact was designed in accordance with Allport's optimal contact conditions and strategies derived from categorization theories. Sixty-one Japanese adults participated in this study. One month after the pre-evaluation, participants in the contact condition engaged in a 15-min interaction with a text-based AI designed to represent a Chinese individual, during which they introduced themselves and discussed possible joint efforts toward achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. The results showed that the contact condition increased explicit measures of positive attitudes and intergroup empathy while reducing negative attitudes relative to the control condition. However, intergroup anxiety and implicit attitudes measured using the Implicit Association Test showed no contact effects. Our findings suggest that a brief, semi-structured contact involving personalized interaction and cooperation task may mitigate some aspects of explicit intergroup bias. This preliminary evidence indicates new possibilities for applying conversational AI in instant messaging environments within intergroup contexts and provides implications for effective e-contact strategies.

candidates.title: Innovative Training Approaches to Codevelop Digital Technologies to Foster Agroecological Practices: Insights from the OccitANum Living Lab
candidates.abstract: Digital technologies can strongly support agroecology transition of the agri-food system as they help optimise inputs, understand complex diversified systems, redesign agroecosystems, and connect farmers with citizens. But adoption remains low, largely due to poor adaptation to real needs, low digital literacy, and lack of trust. Living labs offer an interesting promise to better allow digital technologies use thanks to their structure based on participatory approaches and codesign of solutions with farmers in real-life conditions. Launched in 2020, OccitANum aims at this dual transition, agroecology via digital transformation. It is structured as an archipelago of 15 local Living labs grouped into 7 Open Labs by production sector (livestock, arable crops, vineyard, fruits, vegetables, beekeeping, local food supply) and supported by a central hub (CORE) providing services as facilitator training, data governance support, methodological tools, links with AgTech providers, evaluation frameworks. However, early results of OccitANum were limited because facilitators lacked skills in participatory design, digital maturity among farmers and advisors was low, farmers’ needs were misunderstood or poorly elicited, time and funding constraints hindered engagement. Therefore, to overcome these barriers, OccitANum pivoted toward capacity building through two main systems: (1) the MobiLab, a mobile fablab for hands-on digital learning travelling workshop enabling farmers to discover sensors, to prototype low-cost tools, and to build equipment themselves (so far over 500 participants, ~10 tools developed, dozens of prototypes built); (2) NUMAEE, a digital education for future farmers based on a “digital briefcase” for agricultural teachers to train students in building and using agricultural IoT tools and therefore increase confidence and practical understanding of digital technologies. Based on this momentum, two illustrative achievements are given: (a) the PiLowTech, a DIY soil moisture sensor co-designed with vegetable growers to improve irrigation and (b) the CentipOC network, a farmer-led initiative to deploy an open-source RTK geolocation network across multiple French departments, enabling affordable precision positioning and agriculture. These examples show how low-cost, accessible technologies can catalyse adoption and stimulate collective innovation dynamics. On a step forward, low-tech digital tools can greatly support On-Farm Experimentation, helping farmers test agroecological practices themselves and generate contextualised knowledge. In return, OFE provides real conditions to improve digital tools through iterative, bottom-up design. Thanks to OccitANum, we demonstrate that successful rural digitalisation is not primarily a technical challenge but an ecosystem challenge requiring sustained capacity building, long-term facilitation, alignment of actors, user-centred co-design practices, and tools adapted to real-world agroecological problems. Low-tech, DIY, and participatory approaches emerged as powerful levers to empower farmers and support both the digital and agroecological transitions.

candidates.title: Virtual bodies, real touch: haptic social communication across VR, MR, and cross-reality
candidates.abstract: Introduction Visual and auditory channels in collaborative Extended Reality (XR) can become saturated during complex shared interactions, leaving the potential of social touch–one of the most direct channels for interpersonal communication–largely ignored. This work investigates haptic feedback as a complementary communication channel for supporting social coordination and interpersonal communication across Virtual Reality (VR), Mixed Reality (MR), and cross-reality environments. Methods We present a haptic-enabled multi-user XR system that enables physically distant users to initiate and receive real-time, bidirectional social touch. We developed wearable gloves and forearm sleeves containing 26 vibrotactile actuators distributed across each hand and arm, controlled through a wireless, device-agnostic communication framework. Users can perform and receive social touch gestures, interact with virtual objects, and receive spatially localized vibrotactile feedback. We evaluated our framework with 40 participants forming 20 dyads in a two-part within-subject study. In a prescribed-touch task, participants communicated seven emotions using direct physical touch and mediated touch across VR and MR. We examined how emotion communication differed between physical and mediated touch and whether the realities of the initiator and receiver influenced the interaction. In a free-exploration task, participants interacted unconstrained in VR and MR while we assessed touch behavior, embodiment, presence, social presence, usability, and haptic experience. Results Our results showed that meaningful affective information and emotion-specific gesture patterns were preserved across realities, although direct physical touch produced the strongest affective alignment. The receiver’s reality influenced emotion recognition more strongly than the initiator’s reality, while VR supported longer and more varied touch interactions and MR provided stronger embodiment and perceived usability. Our findings demonstrate that haptic feedback can serve as a critical secondary communication channel for social touch in XR, and our system can support meaningful social touch across heterogeneous realities. Discussion Our findings help derive design implications for improving affective experiences, multisensory interaction, embodiment, and future collaborative XR systems.

candidates.title: Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents
candidates.abstract: developments in contemporary computing, transforming the way intelligent systems understand information, generate content, reason over knowledge, interact with users, and perform complex tasks. The rapid evolution of Large Language Models, multimodal foundation models, retrieval-augmented generation, intelligent agents, and autonomous workflows has created a new generation of AI systems that extend beyond conventional prediction and classification. These developments are influencing software engineering, scientific research, healthcare, education, business, robotics, cybersecurity, manufacturing, and many other domains. The book Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents has been developed to provide a comprehensive academic and engineering-oriented treatment of these emerging technologies. The book approaches Generative AI not merely as a collection of models or tools, but as an engineering discipline involving model architecture, data and knowledge integration, prompting, retrieval, agent orchestration, evaluation, security, deployment, optimization, and responsible operation. The objective is to provide readers with both conceptual foundations and a practical understanding of how modern Generative AI systems are designed and integrated into intelligent applications. The book begins with the foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models. Chapter 1, Foundations of Generative AI and Large Language Models, introduces the evolution of generative modeling from statistical Natural Language Processing to modern foundation models and LLMs. It examines the distinction between discriminative and generative learning and provides a detailed treatment of Transformer architecture, self-attention, multi-head attention, positional encoding, embeddings, and encoder–decoder architectures. The chapter further explores LLM pre-training, next-token prediction, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, parameter-efficient fine-tuning, tokenization, contextual representations, prompting, context engineering, inference optimization, quantization, and model ecosystems. Applications in intelligent tutoring, software engineering, healthcare, scientific knowledge discovery, business intelligence, and customer support establish the practical relevance of LLMs. Chapter 2, LLM Engineering, Retrieval-Augmented Generation, and Multimodal Intelligence, moves from model fundamentals toward application engineering. It explains how LLM APIs, model-serving architectures, prompt templates, structured outputs, function calling, and schema-constrained generation can be integrated into production applications. Particular emphasis is given to Retrieval-Augmented Generation, including document ingestion, chunking, retrieval, reranking, grounding, and knowledge-intensive generation. Advanced retrieval techniques such as hybrid search, dense retrieval, query expansion, query decomposition, graph-based retrieval, and agentic retrieval are examined. The chapter also discusses vector databases, metadata filtering, knowledge graphs, multimodal foundation models, multimodal embeddings, fine-tuning, LoRA, continual adaptation, orchestration frameworks, memory management, and production-oriented architectures. Applications in enterprise knowledge systems, healthcare, scientific research, legal and financial analysis, education, manufacturing, and intelligent search demonstrate the breadth of these technologies. Chapter 3, Intelligent Agents and Agentic AI Engineering, examines the transition from prompt-driven systems to goal-oriented and autonomous AI agents. It introduces reactive, deliberative, and hybrid agent architectures and explains how perception, reasoning, planning, memory, tool use, and action contribute to intelligent behavior. The chapter explores task decomposition, reasoning strategies, reflection, self-correction, decision-making, function calling, external APIs, code execution, search tools, databases, and computational tools. Particular attention is given to short-term and long-term memory, episodic and semantic memory, context compression, persistent memory, and multi-agent collaboration. Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation and autonomous knowledge acquisition are introduced as important mechanisms for developing research-oriented and knowledge-intensive agents. The chapter concludes with agent evaluation, reliability, observability, trajectory analysis, tool-use accuracy, failure analysis, and applications in autonomous software engineering, research, customer service, healthcare, education, finance, and enterprise automation. As Generative AI systems become increasingly capable, their reliability, security, privacy, and responsible deployment become essential. Chapter 4, Secure, Responsible, and Production-Ready Generative AI Engineering, addresses these requirements. It introduces systematic approaches to LLM and application evaluation, benchmarking, human evaluation, automated evaluation, and task-specific assessment. The chapter examines hallucination, factuality, grounded generation, fact verification, confidence estimation, and uncertainty-aware generation. Security topics include prompt injection, jailbreaks, adversarial prompts, data poisoning, model security, and agent security. Privacy-preserving Generative AI is explored through sensitive-data protection, anonymization, federated learning, and privacy-preserving retrieval and inference. The chapter further addresses fairness, bias, explainability, transparency, human oversight, governance, and responsible deployment. Production engineering topics include LLMOps, MLOps, model lifecycle management, prompt and model versioning, monitoring, observability, continuous evaluation, deployment, distributed inference, quantization, distillation, accelerator optimization, and edge AI. Chapter 5, Emerging Trends and Advanced Applications of Generative AI, looks toward the future of the field. It examines reasoning-centric AI models, test-time computation, self-reflection, verification, neuro-symbolic reasoning, and hybrid intelligence. Agentic AI and autonomous workflows are explored through autonomous task execution, human–agent collaboration, workflow automation, and self-improving agent architectures. The chapter also examines Generative AI for software engineering, including coding assistants, automated debugging, software testing, vulnerability detection, and autonomous development agents. Applications in scientific discovery, drug and material design, engineering optimization, clinical decision support, robotics, and embodied intelligence demonstrate the expanding role of Generative AI in the physical and scientific world. The chapter further examines Small Language Models, edge AI, on-device inference, domain-specific foundation models, and energy-efficient Generative AI. Future architectures involving multimodal foundation models, world models, persistent AI memory, collective intelligence, and multi-agent systems are discussed as important directions for next-generation intelligent systems. Finally, emerging applications such as autonomous organizations, personalized education, smart cities, intelligent infrastructure, digital twins, industrial AI, and next-generation human–AI collaboration illustrate the broader societal and technological implications of Generative AI. The engineering lifecycle can therefore be summarized as: Understand → Design → Generate → Retrieve → Reason → Act → Evaluate → Secure → Deploy → Monitor → Improve The book also emphasizes the distinction between generating a plausible output and producing a reliable result. Generative AI systems can produce highly fluent responses while still containing factual errors, unsupported assumptions, security vulnerabilities, or inappropriate recommendations. Consequently, validation, grounding, evaluation, human oversight, and responsible deployment are treated as fundamental engineering requirements rather than optional additions. Another important objective of the book is to establish a bridge between theoretical knowledge and practical system development. Students and professionals need to understand not only how Transformers and LLMs work, but also how these models are incorporated into real applications through APIs, vector databases, retrieval systems, orchestration frameworks, agents, tools, memory systems, and deployment platforms. The book therefore follows a progressive structure that moves from foundations to application engineering, from application engineering to intelligent agents, from agents to secure production systems, and finally toward emerging architectures and advanced applications. The book is intended for undergraduate and postgraduate students of Computer Science and Engineering, Artificial Intelligence, Data Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and related disciplines. It is also designed to support researchers, educators, software engineers, AI practitioners, technology professionals, and readers who wish to develop a systematic understanding of Generative AI engineering. The material can be used for university courses, advanced electives, professional training programs, research preparation, and self-directed learning. The ultimate objective of Generative AI Engineering: Large Language Models and Intelligent Agents is to help readers move from simply using Generative AI tools toward understanding, designing, evaluating, and engineering intelligent systems. Generative AI is becoming an important component of modern computing infrastructure, and its future will depend not only on increasingly capable models but also on the ability to build systems that are reliable, secure, efficient, explainable, scalable, responsible, and human-centered. It is hoped that this book will serve as a useful academic and professional resource for understanding the rapidly developing landscape of Generative AI and will encourage students, researche

candidates.title: Can you give me a hand? A case study of the effect of collaborative robot implementation from an operator perspective
candidates.abstract: Although the implementation of collaborative robots (cobots) in manufacturing has gained significant attention, few studies have examined the challenges operators face throughout the implementation process in real-life production contexts. In response, this study adopted a longitudinal design to investigate the implications of cobot implementation within a brownfield manufacturing setting across three distinct process phases: deployment initiation, operational testing and calibration, and full-scale integration. An exploratory case study was conducted at a Danish multinational company known for its measured approach to automation and strong commitment to job security, which helped reduce potential bias in assessing operators’ perspectives on automation. Data were collected through multiple rounds of semi-structured interviews, enabling the study to capture nuanced insights into operators’ evolving experiences over time. The results contribute to the literature by offering a detailed understanding of the human-centered dynamics of cobot integration, including safety, trust, communication and collaboration, which are critical for addressing implementation barriers. Furthermore, actionable recommendations for enhancing cobot adoption strategies in smart manufacturing are provided, emphasizing the importance of aligning technology integration with operator well-being and organizational practices.

candidates.title: Collective capacity building for emotionally charged work: a grounded theory of strategies for maintaining meaning and well-being in emotionally charged work
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Emotionally charged work-encompassing emotional demands and emotional labour - has been associated with ill health and alienation. While the consequences of such work has been widely theorized, the prevention of negative consequences remains undertheorized. METHODS: In this study, we adopt a classical grounded theory approach to (a) Explore the main concern of employed people regarding emotionally charged work and (b) Generate a grounded theory that could inform sustainable organization of emotionally charged work and the prevention of compassion fatigue. Initial purposeful sampling included eight employees and managers from psychiatric hospitals. As subsequent theoretical sampling required broader diversity, we conducted interviews with 15 additional participants across varied occupations, including ministers of religion, military personnel, social care workers, educators, IT managers, and others. RESULTS: Using open coding and constant comparison, we developed a grounded theory of collective capacity building for emotionally charged work. We found that the main concern of participants was to maintain meaningful working lives and in the context of emotionally charged work, they achieved this by building collective capacity for this work. CONCLUSION: Our findings offer theoretical and practical guidance for sustainably organizing work in occupations marked by high levels of emotionally charged work.

candidates.title: Effects of Transparent Robot Intentions on Human Trust and Compliance in Decision-Making: The Role of Benevolent and Ulterior Intentions of Robots
candidates.abstract: Humans are more commonly relying on the assistance of advanced robots in decision-making processes and may follow robots’ suggestions depending on their understanding of how such suggestions are generated. To enhance human understanding, robots can communicate their (simulated) intentions, influencing the trust placed upon them. However, it remains uncertain whether and under what conditions robots’ simulated intentions could also negatively impact trust and compliance. Therefore, we conducted a laboratory experiment with 182 participants, exploring whether information about a robot’s potential benevolent intentions and ulterior motives increased or decreased trust and compliance with the robot’s suggestions, while also altering participants’ involvement levels in a decision task. The results of two 2x2x2 ANOVAs revealed that, regardless of the involvement level, the robot’s simulated ulterior motives decreased trust and compliance, while benevolent intentions did not significantly affect these outcomes. Thus, simulated intentions should be considered in the design of collaborative decision-making between humans and robots.

candidates.title: TikTok comedy during COVID-19: a multimodal study of platform data, audience engagement, and creative performance
candidates.abstract: This thesis investigates how multimodal features, platform infrastructure, and creative strategy jointly shape audience engagement in TikTok comedy content produced during the COVID-19 period (2020 to 2022). Drawing on a shared corpus of 741 videos from 14 high-profile creators active in the United Kingdom and the United States, three interrelated empirical studies address this aim from complementary analytical angles: evaluating the data infrastructure through which platform content is accessed, modelling how visual, audio, linguistic, and platform features jointly predict audience engagement, and examining how a specific creative strategy independently predicts engagement above and beyond correlated production characteristics. The three studies form a progressive analytical sequence in which each paper establishes the methodological and conceptual foundation for the next. The first paper subjects TikTok’s Research API to the first systematic comparative evaluation of its kind, contrasting its outputs against a commercial third-party analytics service and manual data collection across a broader corpus of 6,373 videos. The API offers genuine strengths, including scalability and access to 22 variables, eight of which are unavailable through alternative methods. The limitations are substantial: transcription coverage reaches approximately ten per cent of content, with systematic demographic skews favouring American male creators, and engagement metrics are inconsistent across data sources. The paper advocates multi-method auditing protocols as a necessary condition of validity for platform-based social science research. The second paper examines how visual composition, audio context, linguistic markers, and platform affordances jointly predict three engagement outcomes in TikTok comedy videos, using Generalised Additive Mixed Models with creator-specific random intercepts. Likes, comments, and shares respond to qualitatively distinct multimodal configurations rather than a single underlying engagement factor. Likes function as sensory verdicts, sensitive to visual composition and prosodic expressiveness. Comments reflect cognitive verdicts, driven by video duration, title sentiment, and linguistic complexity. Shares embody social verdicts, shaped by relationship-focused content, transcript sentiment, and lexical accessibility. Video description length is the sole universal predictor across all three models. Creator gender consistently moderates multimodal effects throughout. The third paper investigates role-play, a comedic strategy in which creators explicitly embody characters distinct from their everyday personas, accounting for 57.4 per cent of the corpus. Role-play videos display a consistent and identifiable production signature, characterised by significantly higher rates of accessory use, distinct costuming, and relationship-focused narratives. Role-play independently predicts approximately 21 per cent higher like counts and 42 to 48 per cent higher share counts after controlling for the full production feature set, yet shows no significant independent effect on comment counts. Male creators derive substantially greater sharing gains from same-gender role-play than female creators, a pattern consistent with accounts of gender-incongruent performance in algorithmically mediated contexts. Across the three papers, two findings recur with sufficient consistency to constitute thesis-level contributions. Engagement on TikTok is irreducibly multidimensional: likes, comments, and shares are driven by distinct feature configurations and cannot be collapsed into a single outcome measure without substantial loss of analytical precision. Creator gender is a structural moderating variable that shapes not only baseline engagement levels but the mechanisms through which multimodal features and creative strategies translate into audience response. Together, the three studies advance multimodal communication theory, extend performance and gender performativity frameworks into short-form digital contexts, and contribute to an emerging methodological literature on the conditions of validity for platform-based social science.

candidates.title: Robotics and Trust
candidates.abstract: Imagine you would be hanging on a cliff—Would you take a robot’s hand? Though the imagination of one hanging on a cliff seems dramatic, it well demonstrates a situation of vulnerability in which a person needs to rely on another’s capability and integrity to help him or her. As the number of service robots in various fields increases enormously, see [ 74 ], it is likely that people will find themselves in situations of vulnerability in which they depend on robotic assistance. As such, robots cannot be merely regarded as tools performing repetitive tasks. Instead, robots’ role as embodied social agents that are attributed with intentions and morality gains importance. This calls for a clear understanding of trust in HRI which needs to be well distinguished from trust in automation, see [ 41 ] for a review. The best way to achieve this is to understand trust in interpersonal relationships first.

candidates.title: AI BASED HAND GESTURE CONTROLLED ROBOT
candidates.abstract: The proposed system presents an advanced AI-based hand gesture controlled telepresence robot designed for operation in hazardous and inaccessible environments. The system enables a remote operator to control a robotic rover using real-time hand gestures without the need for physical controllers or wearable devices. It integrates computer vision techniques using OpenCV and MediaPipe for accurate skeletal hand tracking and gesture recognition. A dual-processing architecture ensures efficient handling of high-definition video streaming and gesture interpretation with minimal latency. The robot provides real-time visual feedback through wireless video transmission, enabling safe navigation and monitoring. The system ensures intuitive control, improved safety, and enhanced operational efficiency. This solution is highly applicable in disaster management, industrial inspection, and healthcare environments where human presence is risky or limited.

candidates.title: Implementing robotic-assisted therapy in stroke rehabilitation: a structured narrative review of evidence and technology adoption barriers in Indonesia
candidates.abstract: Introduction Robotic-assisted therapy (RAT) has emerged as a promising intervention for post-stroke recovery; however, its implementation in developing countries such as Indonesia remains limited by economic, technical, and systemic barriers. This structured narrative review summarizes clinical effect reported by systematics review and meta-analyses and examines implementation consideration and potential economic feasibility within the Indonesian healthcare context. Method A structured review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses (2015–2025) was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, PEDro, and Cochrane Library. Studies involving adult with stroke were included. Findings were synthesized narratively because of heterogeneity. Implementation barriers were analyzed, and a scenario-based economic model was developed to assess feasibility of RAT in Indonesia. QALY-equivalent outcomes (QEOs) were estimated using ratio-based value-transfer approach that scaled published reference values according to observed functional effects. Result Evidence from 22 systematic reviews indicated that RAT improved functional outcomes compared with conventional therapy, particularly gait and upper-limb function (effect sizes: 0.02–0.52). Key implementation barriers included limited device availability, inadequate workforce training, and regulatory constraints. Modelled ICERs ranged from US$236.23–752.31 per QEO for upper-limb rehabilitation and US$558.86–4,890 per QEO for gait-related rehabilitation. Most estimates remained below the Indonesian willingness-to-pay threshold ( Conclusion RAT shows potential clinical benefits, but implementation in Indonesia should consider clinical effectiveness, economic feasibility, infrastructure, workforce, technology acceptance, and reimbursement. A phased approach in suitable tertiary-care settings may support wider adoption based on local evidence.

candidates.title: AI-based task-scheduling advice: the associations between adoption intent, AI anthropomorphism, and perceived competence fit
candidates.abstract: Recent studies have suggested that user adoption of AI-based outputs may be positively related to AI agent anthropomorphism, with perceived agent competence serving as a mediator. This paper examines those relationships in the novel, general-purpose context of AI-based task-scheduling advice, which guides users in their daily activities. Path analyses were conducted across two scenario-based studies (Study 1, N = 258; Study 2, N = 194), which presented AI-based apps. Both studies indicated positive associations between perceived agent anthropomorphism and advice adoption, with a mediated path through perceived competence agent-advice fit. Moreover, Study 2 indicated positive associations between a user's individual tendency to anthropomorphize and advice adoption intent, with a mediated path through perceived agent anthropomorphism and perceived competence agent-advice fit. These results extend the knowledge about user response to AI by demonstrating associations between AI anthropomorphism, perceived competence, and adoption intent in the area of task-scheduling advice, and by applying anthropomorphizing tendency as a user characteristic involved in these associations. These findings can guide practitioners on how users may respond to AI-based task-scheduling advice.

Sustainability cost of defect engineering in color centers for quantum communications
candidates.abstract: Quantum communication relies on optically active color centers for scalable spin-photon networking, yet the sustainability implications of defect engineering remain largely unexplored. We comparatively evaluate twenty host crystal-defect generation combinations across diamond, SiC, h-BN, GaN, ZnO using ion implantation, e-beam irradiation, laser writing, and heteroepitaxial growth techniques. A multi-attribute cradle-to-gate framework integrating life cycle, chemical hazard, human health toxicity, and technoeconomic assessments reveals distinct thermodynamic, chemical, health, and economic tradeoffs emerge across defect engineering pathways. h-BN paired with laser writing shows the lowest overall burdens, with low energy demand, global warming potential <20 kg CO2 eq./chip, minimal hazard/toxicity profiles, and lowest fabrication cost. SiC provides a balanced near-term pathway by retaining strong quantum functionality while moderating sustainability burdens. ZnO and GaN show selective process-level advantages for integrated photonics, whereas diamond remains burden-intensive due to energy-demanding growth and complex post-defect stabilization requirements. Identified greener interventions enable scalable and resource-conscious quantum communication hardware. Sustainable manufacturing is becoming an increasingly important consideration for emerging quantum technologies. Here, the authors assess the environmental, chemical, human-health, and economic impacts of defect engineering strategies for color-center platforms used in quantum communications, highlighting trade-offs between quantum functionality and resource demands while identifying lower-impact solutions.

candidates.title: Loneliness to consumption intention: emotional bonding and escapism in AI emotional companion app use
candidates.abstract: With the diffusion of generative AI, AI emotional companion apps have emerged as a new domain of digital consumption in which users may pay to extend relationship-like experiences. This study examines how loneliness and actual-ideal self-discrepancy are associated with experience-enhancing consumption intention and continuance intention through two competing pathways: emotional bonding with the AI (relational compensation) and escapism (avoidant compensation). The emotional bond with the AI is modeled as a second-order construct comprising anthropomorphism, emotional responsiveness, and parasocial intimacy. Data were collected from 393 adult users in China who used AI emotional companion apps at least twice per week and were analyzed using structural equation modeling. Loneliness and actual-ideal self-discrepancy were positively associated with both emotional bonding and escapism. However, significant indirect associations with experience-enhancing consumption intention and continuance intention emerged only through the emotional-bond pathway. Direct comparisons further showed that the relational indirect effects were significantly stronger than the avoidant indirect effects across all antecedent–outcome combinations. Escapism was significantly associated with both outcomes when modeled alone but became nonsignificant when emotional bonding was included, suggesting that its association with consumer responses largely overlaps with the relational pathway. A partial-mediation analysis further showed that actual-ideal self-discrepancy retained a significant direct association with continuance intention. These findings suggest that relational compensation, rather than avoidant compensation, is more closely associated with willingness to pay for experience enhancement and intention to continue using AI companions. The study extends compensatory-use, self-discrepancy, and parasocial-interaction perspectives to the AI-companion context by linking psychological vulnerability to experience-enhancing consumption intention and continuance intention, while highlighting implications for responsible relational design and user protection.

candidates.title: “Serve Them with Rituals”: Power and Emotions in the Confucian Parent-Child Relationship
candidates.abstract: This article challenges the conventional portrayal of the parent-child relationship in Confucian thought as authoritarian and even oppressive. It reconstructs a Confucian ethical view of the relationship from the perspective of parenting in addition to the more common discussions of filial conduct. It argues that the Analects ’ view of filial conduct emphasizes following ritual norms instead of absolute obedience to parents. Although the Analects does not explicitly discuss parenting, passages that mention Confucius with his children are thought provoking. By examining the role of emotions and power dynamics in rituals involving the parent-child relationship, the article defends an account of how Confucian ritual cultivates appropriate love and respect on the part of both parents and children, and its intention is to restrain the conduct of the more powerful in such unequal relationships, instead of oppressing the vulnerable.

EIGR-infer: a blockchain-governed framework for decentralised LLM inference via encrypted intent-guided routing, semantic sharding, and four novel privacy mechanisms
candidates.abstract: Abstract The dominance of centralized cloud providers in large language model (LLM) inference compels users to transmit sensitive queries to third-party servers, sacrificing data privacy and introducing systemic single points of failure. This paper presents EIGR-Infer —a decentralised inference framework that distributes LLM execution across a heterogeneous peer-to-peer (P2P) mesh of consumer-grade edge devices including smartphones, laptops, and local GPU workstations. The framework’s foundational contribution is the encrypted intent-guided routing (EIGR) protocol, which resolves the Finder’s Dilemma: how to direct a query to the semantically appropriate model shard without revealing the query’s content to the routing network. EIGR achieves this through three coordinated mechanisms: on-device semantic intent hashing using HKDF-SHA256 over a local cosine-similarity projection, Kademlia-DHT-based expert shard discovery keyed on the non-invertible hash, and chaos-adaptive onion routing for encrypted delivery. Beyond EIGR, this paper introduces four entirely novel, previously unpublished contributions: (1) DP-SSIM, a Differentially private semantic intent mapping construction providing formal $$(\varepsilon ,\delta )$$ -DP guarantees on routing metadata; (2) the ghost shard protocol (GSP), a deceptive defence mechanism using cryptographically indistinguishable fake shard announcements to deter and detect model-extraction adversaries; (3) federated domain centroid consensus (FDCC), a Byzantine-fault-tolerant gossip protocol for maintaining the shared domain vocabulary without any central authority; and (4) session-adaptive shard re-routing (SASR), a mid-session semantic drift detection and shard migration mechanism for high-quality private multi-turn inference. All seven algorithms are formally specified and analysed. Discrete-event simulation across a 1000-node heterogeneous mesh demonstrates EIGR discovery latency of 47 ms at the 95th percentile, end-to-end inference latency of 460 ms for 512-token prompts, DP-SSIM overhead below 2 ms, ghost shard detection rate of 98.3%, FDCC convergence within 3–4 gossip rounds, and SASR re-routing latency of 31 ms—all compatible with interactive inference targets.
